firms.name: Jane Street
firms.langs: Any language. OCaml explicitly NOT required or rewarded.
firms.oa: None standard for SWE
firms.pipeline_intern: Resume read by a human -> 1 live screen (45-60 min, CoderPad or non-runnable editor) -> 3 x ~45 min coding rounds, 2 interviewers each. Can be cut mid-day.
firms.pipeline_ft: 1-2 live screens -> 3 x ~1 h coding rounds (2 interviewers each) + project deep-dive ('walk through a system you built'); senior adds a design discussion. No behavioural rounds for engineers.
themes: One problem per round, extended in 2-3 escalating parts
Games / state machines / small data structures
Code must be correct without running it
Clean readable code + communication weighted as heavily as the answer
firms.verdict: The most distinctive loop in the industry. No OA, no puzzles for devs, no LeetCode copy-paste. Part 2 of each question usually breaks your part-1 design.

sources.t: Official: preparing for a SWE interview

roleNotes.dev: No online assessment. One live screen then 3 coding rounds, two interviewers each. Any language; OCaml explicitly not required. One problem per round, extended 2-3 times. Officially: 'no mental math, math-olympiad questions, or logic puzzles' for devs.
roleNotes.researcher: Phone screen on maths/probability (Python coding for some tracks), then 1-2 technical rounds, then a 3-5 round onsite. Coding is 'real world generalist work, like optimizing an I/O function or processing datasets', with complexity analysis but not isolated algorithm questions.
roleNotes.trader: NO CODING AT ALL. 2-3 conversational phone calls built around linked betting and strategy games (dice, cards, coins); pen and paper allowed, no calculators. Full day onsite where candidates receive 100 poker chips and bet them on their answers.

firms.name: Citadel Securities
firms.langs: C++ or Python. C++ internals grilled if C++ is on your resume.
firms.oa: HackerRank 2-3 problems, 60-90 min
firms.pipeline_intern: HackerRank OA (2-3 problems, 60-90 min) -> 1-2 CoderPad rounds (first mixes resume/behavioural + one coding problem) -> superday 3-4 rounds -> team matching.
firms.pipeline_ft: Usually no OA. Recruiter -> 1-2 CoderPad screens (LeetCode medium + C++ conceptual) -> superday 4-6 rounds incl. a ~2 h 'comprehend and optimise obfuscated C++' round -> team matching. Single weak round can end the day.
themes: STL internals, move semantics, smart pointers, vtables, std::variant
Order book BBO/NBBO, matching engine
Read-and-optimise someone else's C++
Escalation: 'now make it faster / thread-safe / handle load'
firms.verdict: FAANG algorithms plus a genuine C++/systems bar. Team matching means a clean loop can still end without an offer.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank OA (2-3 problems, 60-90 min) then CoderPad screens mixing a LeetCode-medium with C++ internals, then a superday including the ~2 hour 'comprehend and optimise obfuscated C++' round. Then team matching.
roleNotes.researcher: HackerRank OA of ~80 min mixing coding (LeetCode medium-hard), probability puzzles and multiple-choice statistics/ML. Then a 45 min technical-plus-behavioural first round on CoderPad, then 3-5 x 60 min onsite with a research deep-dive.
roleNotes.trader: 'Trader 101' OA: 30 minutes, four sections of statistics and probability. Then phone rounds mixing brainteasers and EV, a market-making game where the interviewer trades against your quotes, and a superday. Coding is minimal.

firms.name: G-Research
firms.langs: C# shop historically; take-home in any language. Python/C++ for research.
firms.oa: 90-min Quant Quiz (10 MCQ) for QR; automated coding OA for SWE
firms.pipeline_intern: QR: same online quant quiz -> 3 technical interviews compressed into one day + mentor interviews. SWE: automated coding OA -> assessment centre + mentor interviews.
firms.pipeline_ft: QR: Quant Quiz (90 min) -> 1 h triage interview (harder than the quiz) -> 3-4 x 1 h technicals (one deep maths + two of programming/stats/ML/finance) -> management. SWE: ~2 h take-home -> full day or two half-days onsite.
themes: Probability, OLS, linear algebra, ODEs dominate for QR
Distinctive round: improve code performance by reading only the logs
Take-home reviewed like a code review with a colleague
Kubernetes/Ansible for platform roles
firms.verdict: Maths-first for research; the coding bar is 'code you can defend line by line', not LeetCode volume. Quiz time management is a documented failure mode.

roleNotes.dev: A take-home of a single question that should take about two hours, in any language, then a full day or two half-days onsite. Includes the distinctive 'improve performance by reading only the logs' round, plus Kubernetes/Ansible for platform roles.
roleNotes.researcher: 90-minute Quant Quiz (10 multiple-choice, 5 options each) on probability, statistics, linear algebra, calculus and finance. Then a 1 hour triage interview, harder than the quiz. Then 3-4 x 1 hour technicals: one deep maths plus two of programming, statistics, ML or finance. Then management rounds.

firms.name: XTX Markets
firms.langs: C++ essentially required for core engineering; Python for research; Go for some platform.
firms.oa: TestGorilla 20 questions / 60 min (Junior QR); take-home for SWE
firms.pipeline_intern: Risk intern official template: ~90 min take-home + 2 x 45 min interviews. SWE intern loop not publicly reported - infer OA/take-home + 2 technicals.
firms.pipeline_ft: QR: 20-problem/60-min online test (no back-navigation) -> 4-5 researcher interviews -> Kaggle-style take-home with 3 submissions -> up to 10 rounds over 2 days. SWE: ~30 min rapid-fire C++/OS phone screen -> evening take-home -> 5 x 1 h onsite (LeetCode-hard + system design).
themes: Rapid-fire C++/OS trivia at phone-screen speed
Take-home graded on robustness, not minimal correctness
ML from first principles, whiteboard derivations
'Strong in all areas, exceptional in one'
firms.verdict: Broadest bar of any firm here. A couple of weak answers in any round ends it. One documented rejection: take-home 'too simple, should have addressed other factors'.

roleNotes.dev: ~30 minute voice-only phone screen of roughly 20 rapid-fire C++, compiler and OS questions with no time to think. Then an evening take-home, then 5 x 1 hour onsite with LeetCode-hard problems and system design.
roleNotes.researcher: 20 problems in 60 minutes on TestGorilla (probability, linear algebra, calculus, algorithms, brainteasers) with no back-navigation. Then 4-5 researcher interviews, a Kaggle-style take-home with 3 submissions, then up to 10 rounds over 2 days.

firms.name: Quadrature Capital
firms.langs: Python (take-home) and C++.
firms.oa: Long Python take-home (up to ~8 h reported)
firms.pipeline_intern: Skills test / OA + phone -> up to 4 interviews of algorithmic and implementation questions. No finance knowledge expected. Quant-dev intern is the fastest process (~21 days).
firms.pipeline_ft: Informal call -> take-home Python task (reports up to 8 h) -> half-day London onsite, 2-3 collaborative 'work with your interviewer' sessions -> second day with directors, ending with the CEO.
themes: Collaborative, evolving-requirements pairing (two-on-one)
Heavy runtime analysis on LeetCode medium->hard
Streaming data structures (median via heaps)
Cache-aware trade-offs even for pure devs
firms.verdict: Thinnest public evidence of the priority eight - candidates cite an NDA. Expect to be surprised by format; prepare for shifting requirements rather than a fixed question bank.

roleNotes.dev: Quadrature uses one title, Quant Developer, for both research and technology work, so there is no separate researcher or trader loop. Take-home Python task (reports of up to 8 hours), then a half-day onsite of 2-3 collaborative sessions, then a second day ending with the CEO.
roleNotes.researcher: Not a separate track. Research sits inside the Quant Developer role, so researchers go through the same take-home and collaborative onsite as engineers.

firms.name: PDT Partners
firms.langs: C++ (dedicated round for campus SWE); Python.
firms.oa: No OA reported; 1 h engineer screen
firms.difficulty: SWE: moderate (rated PDT's easiest). QR: very high
firms.pipeline_intern: SWE/Systems intern: 1 h engineer screen with one LeetCode easy/medium (iterators) -> campus loop of algorithm round (two related DP problems) + dedicated C++ round + experience round. Fast. NO QR internship exists.
firms.pipeline_ft: QR (PhD only): ~30 min phone -> 2 technical + hiring-partner round -> NYC superday with research talk, probability/stats/brainteasers, open-ended 'mini-project' questions, and a long hard written test. A Mar 2026 take-home: 'not expected to finish', outside sources OK, no LLM.
themes: SWE track is notably lighter than peers
QR track described as harder than Citadel or Two Sigma
Open-ended problems, each its own mini project
Assembly/Linux/C++ written exam for systems roles
firms.verdict: The clearest dev-vs-research split of any firm here. Interns get an easy loop; researchers get one of the hardest processes in the industry.

roleNotes.dev: Notably lighter than peers and rated PDT's easiest loop. A 1 hour engineer screen with one LeetCode easy/medium on iterators, then a campus loop of an algorithm round (two related DP problems), a dedicated C++ round, and an experience round.
roleNotes.researcher: PhD only, full-time, and no internship exists. ~30 min phone, 2 technical rounds plus a hiring partner, then an NYC superday with a research talk, probability and statistics, open-ended 'mini project' questions, and a long written test. Reported as harder than Citadel or Two Sigma.

firms.name: TGS Management
firms.langs: Not clearly reported.
firms.oa: None reported
firms.pipeline_intern: No internship programme. New-grad hiring only recently started.
firms.pipeline_ft: QR: two 1 h phone/Zoom screens (background + brainteasers; one report of 'one data structure question and one statistics question') -> background-heavy onsite including 'computer system questions'. Process length ranges 16 days to 2 months; ghosting and late Irvine-relocation disclosure reported.
themes: Brainteasers and combinatorics dominate
Very few verbatim questions exist publicly
Coding-round claim is weakly evidenced
firms.verdict: Thinnest evidence of all eight priority firms - only two verbatim questions on record, one from 2014. Treat any confident guide about TGS with suspicion.

roleNotes.dev: Thin evidence. One report of a resume design-decision deep-dive with no coding.
roleNotes.researcher: Two 1 hour phone screens (background plus brainteasers; one report of 'one data structure question and one statistics question'), then a background-heavy onsite including 'computer system questions'. Only two verbatim questions exist publicly.

firms.name: Radix Trading
firms.langs: C++ required in QR screens. Python also used.
firms.oa: None reported; live technical screens
firms.pipeline_intern: PhD QR intern track looks identical to full-time. SWE intern: HR call -> technical phone screen with classics (e.g. reverse a linked list).
firms.pipeline_ft: QR: 15 min recruiter screen -> virtual round on probability + algorithms (C++ required) -> Chicago superday of 3-6 rounds including co-founders and a 45-60 min academic-style research talk.
themes: Probability derivations sit alongside algorithms
C++ required even in research screens
Research presentation is a formal round
Complexity analysis explicitly requested
firms.verdict: Research-heavy but with a real coding bar in C++. The widely-repeated 'tick data take-home' is asserted only by prep sites with no first-hand confirmation.

roleNotes.dev: HR call then a technical phone screen with classics such as reversing a linked list. Thinner evidence than the research track.
roleNotes.researcher: 15 min recruiter screen, then a virtual round on probability and algorithms with C++ required, then a Chicago superday of 3-6 rounds including co-founders and a 45-60 minute academic-style research talk.

firms.name: Hudson River Trading
firms.langs: C++ or Python (separate postings). Some intern OAs have been C++-only. AI tools explicitly prohibited.
firms.oa: CodeSignal / Codility, 3-4 problems, 90-120 min; ALL hidden tests must pass
firms.difficulty: Very high (OA is the big filter)
firms.pipeline_intern: OA within days of applying (3 problems; systems intern got Codility 90 min inside a 2.5 h window, C/C++/Python/Go only) -> 1-2 technical calls. Systems intern gets a 45-min NO-CODING call on Linux, C++ pointers/memory, Python/Bash.
firms.pipeline_ft: CodeSignal OA (Algo Dev: 2 h, 3 questions, third harder than LeetCode-hard) -> phone 1 (30-45 min, systems/C++ trivia, often zero algorithms) -> phone 2 (60 min live coding) -> onsite 4-6 rounds / up to 6.5 h: coding, research/data-science (pandas), open-ended design absorbing changing requirements, OS/systems, behavioural.
themes: Phone screen is pure C++/OS: inline, vector vs list, malloc, sbrk vs mmap, demand paging
Correct-but-slow = rejected. TLE is a fail
Order book with O(1) cancel; HRT publishes its own book-builder exercise
Probability done exactly (DP), not by Monte Carlo
firms.verdict: Officially: 'we stray away from burst-of-insight LeetCode questions' and want strong fundamentals. In practice the OA is a brutal all-tests-must-pass filter and the phone screen is systems trivia.

roleNotes.dev: CodeSignal or Codility OA (3-4 problems, all hidden tests must pass), then a phone screen that is pure C++/OS trivia with often no algorithms at all, then a live coding call, then a 4-6 round onsite of up to 6.5 hours.
roleNotes.researcher: The Algo Developer track is essentially quant research. Same OA, but the loop adds a research and maths phone screen (probability, Bayes, distributions) and a data-science onsite round using pandas and prediction tasks. Python rather than C++.

firms.name: Jump Trading
firms.langs: C++ emphasised for engineering; Python for research/infra.
firms.oa: HackerRank/Codility 2-3 hard problems, 90-120 min
firms.pipeline_intern: QR intern: NO OA - HR call, then a round with coding plus a trading-strategy/game-theory problem, then a further round. Quant summer intern OA (2020): 3 questions / 105 min on Codility.
firms.pipeline_ft: HackerRank OA with hard DP and graph problems -> HR/background round -> technical rounds. Core-dev roles add kernel, concurrency and CPU-architecture questions. A take-home order-book exercise has been used for SWE hires.
themes: Implementation-heavy Codility problems
Hash map / trie / linked list from scratch
Real take-home order book with recovered message formats
Concurrency and CPU architecture
firms.verdict: Interviews reportedly 'don't go beyond LeetCode-medium' but the OA does. C++ semantics (move, refcount, I/O) come up repeatedly.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank or Codility OA with hard DP and graph problems, then rounds on C++ semantics (move, reference counting, I/O). Core-dev roles add kernel, concurrency and CPU-architecture questions. A take-home order book has been used.
roleNotes.researcher: NO online assessment for QR interns. Three rounds: an HR call, a round mixing coding with a trading-strategy or game-theory problem, then a further round. Full-time QR gets a 1 hour Python block on simulation, pricing or data manipulation.

firms.name: Tower Research Capital
firms.langs: C++ and Python.
firms.oa: HackerRank ~1 h, 3 sections
firms.pipeline_intern: HackerRank 1 h in 3 sections: 3 DSA (Codeforces 1600-1800), probability/maths, and C++/Python OOP + computer architecture. R1: LeetCode medium/hard + probability puzzles + pandas details. R2 fundamentals round.
firms.pipeline_ft: MCQ OA + 4 coding (SQL, find the Python bug, parsing, algorithm) -> interviews on TLB and huge pages, RISC vs CISC, shared vs static libraries, syscalls at assembly level, pipelining/branch prediction. Pod-specific; experienced hires report tricky basic coding rather than senior system design.
themes: Computer architecture rapid-fire (TLB, pipelining, branch prediction)
Parallel prefix-sum with p threads
Sort a very large array with limited RAM
Probability sits inside the same OA as DSA
firms.verdict: One of the few firms testing computer architecture explicitly. Final day mixes systems design, competitive programming, quant puzzles and project discussion.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank of 1 hour in three sections: 3 DSA problems at Codeforces 1600-1800, probability and maths, and C++/Python OOP plus computer architecture. Later rounds go deep on TLB, huge pages, pipelining and branch prediction.
roleNotes.researcher: Round 1 mixes LeetCode medium/hard with probability puzzles and pandas details. Campus rounds are described as competitive programming, probability and markets.
roleNotes.trader: Campus rounds cover competitive programming, probability and markets; evidence is thinner than for the dev track.

firms.name: Optiver
firms.langs: C++ dominant (OA also accepts Java/Python); C# for GUI roles. Python reportedly not accepted on some SWE OAs.
firms.oa: HackerRank 2-3 problems, 90-120 min + OOP MCQ + Zap-N games
firms.pipeline_intern: SWE intern OA: 2 coding problems (~2 h) or one 75-min 'implement this spec' + 20-min MCQ (DSA, networks, SQL, system design) + Zap-N reaction games. Loop: behavioural -> tech screen -> algorithmic round -> system design -> second behavioural. QT/QR intern: 80 arithmetic questions in 8 min, sequences, 10 probability questions at 90 s each, personality test, group Fermi estimation, card-game strategy. NO coding for QT interns.
firms.pipeline_ft: Graduate SWE OA: HackerRank 2 problems / 120 min + 10 MCQ / 20 min (OOP) + Zap-N ~1 h -> recruiter behavioural -> technical (resume + DS&A, must explain and optimise) -> superday: resume + OOP coding in C++, then system-design discussion. Experienced: coding, experience review, design, behavioural, CTO.
themes: OA reuses a small problem bank across years
Long 'story' specs with starter classes - scope management, not algorithms
Code style is scored: 90% correctness rejected while 77.8% progressed
Amsterdam->Frankfurt latency design appears at every level
firms.verdict: Least algorithm-trivia of the big market makers, most object-oriented design. Hidden tests plus a style score means passing tests is not enough.

sources.t: First-hand: principal SWE loop with written feedback

roleNotes.dev: OA of 2-3 coding problems plus an OOP multiple-choice section plus Zap-N reaction games. Then behavioural, a technical round where you must explain and optimise, and a superday with OOP coding in C++ and a verbal system-design discussion.
roleNotes.researcher: Take-home projects are reported as central and 'much closer to the day-to-day work of a Quant Researcher', but this rests on prep-company sources rather than first-hand reports.
roleNotes.trader: NO CODING. 80 arithmetic questions in 8 minutes with +1/-1 scoring, sequence and pattern games, 10 probability questions at 90 seconds each, and a personality test. Then group Fermi estimation and card-game strategy interviews.

firms.name: IMC Trading
firms.langs: C++ (hot path) or Java track chosen at recruiter screen; Python for quant-dev/data.
firms.oa: HackerRank 2 questions, 105-120 min
firms.difficulty: High; C++ internals are the differentiator
firms.pipeline_intern: HackerRank OA (2 questions) -> one-way video (5 questions: 2 behavioural + 3 technical, 45 s read + 3 min answer) -> campus loop with a GROUP CODE REVIEW of a C++ ResourceManager/order-processing snippet -> 90-min technical (30 min discussing the optimal order-book approach, 60 min coding it) -> HR.
firms.pipeline_ft: HackerRank OA (2 medium-hard in 120 min) -> one-way video -> final Zoom/onsite. Onsite coding is 'always the same question': implement a matching engine from skeleton code against 20-44 pre-written unit tests (add order, delete, partial fills, multi-level sweeps). You are told not to expect to finish.
themes: Matching engine at every stage, from OA to final round
Stack-with-increment family (LeetCode 1381 variants)
Knight-BFS family
Smart pointer internals, vtable layout, false sharing
firms.verdict: Graded on unit-test pass rate AND on following the interviewer's intended approach - a candidate who passed all 44 tests was still rejected.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank OA (2 questions, 105-120 min), a one-way video round, then an onsite whose coding station is 'always' building a matching engine from skeleton code against 20-44 pre-written unit tests. Interns get a group C++ code review instead of deep trivia.
roleNotes.trader: Neurolympics cognitive games (~45 min), a maths and probability test, and a one-way video defining eigenvalues, survivor bias and conditional probability. Then HR and an Amsterdam superday with dice and cards probability, a market-making game and options basics. Reported as 'not about coding at all'.

firms.name: SIG (Susquehanna)
firms.langs: Developer OA: C++/Java/Python/C#. Trader track: basic Python only.
firms.oa: CodeSignal 4 questions ~70 min (2 easy + 2 hard); trader maths exam 14 Q / 20 min
firms.pipeline_intern: QT programme: maths entrance exam (14 questions / 20 min) -> HR-led round with 5 probability questions. NO CODING for the trader track. SWE/Trading Systems intern: OA of C++ string/array problems -> phone screen doing joins/merges/aggregates in numpy/pandas -> superday: implement std::vector from scratch, a system design round, and a maths round.
firms.pipeline_ft: Recruiter -> CodeSignal (4 questions: 2 easy + 2 very hard) -> virtual onsite (OOD + live coding) -> onsite (team fit, resume deep-dive, managers). Some rounds are pure discussion with no LeetCode; heavily team-dependent.
themes: Developer OA is implementation/unit-test driven, not algorithmic
implement std::vector from scratch is the canonical C++ question
pandas/numpy fluency for trading-systems roles
OOD/SOLID design round; escalation via 'extend the class'
firms.verdict: Insider advice: know when and where to use data structures; you do not need the single optimal solution. Trader track failures are attributed to probability, not code.

roleNotes.dev: CodeSignal (4 questions, 2 easy and 2 very hard) or a unit-test-driven OA that is deliberately not algorithmic. Then a 60-90 min coding and optimisation round and an OOD round requiring an extensible SOLID design. Trading Systems interns get implement-std::vector plus a pandas phone screen.
roleNotes.researcher: A 1 hour 'Problem Solving Assessment' of 15 questions covering probability, statistics, brainteasers and single-variable calculus.
roleNotes.trader: NO CODING AT ANY STAGE. A 14-question, 20-minute maths entrance exam, then an HR-led round of 5 probability questions, then a superday of poker and game-theory flavoured EV work and market-making.

firms.name: Akuna Capital
firms.langs: C++ dominant; Python, Java, C#. Take-home in C++.
firms.oa: HackerRank 3 problems, 60-90 min + C++17/20 MCQ
firms.pipeline_intern: C++ SWE intern: HackerRank 80 min, 3 problems (market-order tracker, data throttler, one more) + ~10 MCQs on C++17/20 syntax and code tracing. Python intern (Sydney): ~120 min, 10 CS MCQs + warm-up + coin-change variant. C++ track then gets a debugging round; Python track a build-from-scratch round.
firms.pipeline_ft: OA (3 problems 60-90 min + C++ MCQ) -> 72-HOUR TAKE-HOME MATCHING ENGINE -> phone screen(s) -> onsite (coding, system design, projects). Junior QR: HackerRank 3 LeetCode-mediums, do any 2, explicitly graded on cleanliness and readability -> one-way video maths exam (5 questions x 5 min) -> live probability round.
themes: Order book / matching engine at every stage
72-h take-home graded on hidden tests with a 2-s limit - std::cin throughput decides the last cases
Sliding-window throttlers and streaming statistics
C++ value semantics: move assignment, RAII, object-pool concurrency bugs
firms.verdict: Explicit code-cleanliness grading. One rejection cited needing 'even stronger proficiency in probability and statistics, as well as strong coding skills'.

sources.t: GfG: Akuna C++ SWE intern round 1

roleNotes.dev: OA of 3 problems in 60-90 min plus C++17/20 multiple choice, then the 72-hour take-home matching engine, then phone screens and an onsite covering coding, system design and projects.
roleNotes.researcher: HackerRank of 3 LeetCode-mediums, solve any two, explicitly graded on cleanliness and readability. Then a one-way video maths exam of 5 questions at 5 minutes each, then a live probability round on CodePair.
roleNotes.trader: Two OAs (trader arithmetic and sequences, then 3 LeetCode easy-medium problems), then a webcam maths round of 7 timed probability questions, then trader interviews.

firms.name: DRW
firms.langs: Java or C++ expected. Extra points for solving in C++.
firms.oa: Codility 3 questions / 150 min (120 min for experienced C++)
firms.pipeline_intern: Codility OA, 3 questions / 150 min, partial credit for partially correct. More points if at least one of three is in C++. Then team-specific interviews - each team interviews separately.
firms.pipeline_ft: New grad: Codility 3/150 -> phone -> team interviews. Experienced C++: OA 3 C++ questions / 120 min (one 'find the bug in this snippet', two LeetCode medium-hard) -> 1 h technical. Senior: recruiter -> two remote technical rounds -> TAKE-HOME (Tetris engine) -> remote coding -> Chicago onsite of 5 rounds where you extend your take-home live. One recruiter: 'no algo live coding round'.
themes: Codility with strict O(N) performance tests
Ad-hoc/greedy/simulation problems more than classic DP
Take-home extended live at the onsite
Endianness/serialisation, TCP/IP, virtual memory
firms.verdict: Team-by-team variance is the defining feature. Experienced loops replace LeetCode with a take-home plus open-ended systems questions.

roleNotes.dev: Codility OA of 3 questions in 150 minutes with partial credit and extra points for C++. Experienced loops replace live algorithms with a take-home (a Tetris engine) that you then extend live at a 5-round Chicago onsite.
roleNotes.researcher: Quant dev rounds mix merge sort, dice-game expected value, a graph problem and window functions over time series, with the hardest question required in C++.

firms.name: Flow Traders
firms.langs: C++11/14 and Java.
firms.oa: HackerRank ~12 questions, ~2 h (>half programming); trader maths 75 Q / 10 min
firms.difficulty: High; OA is the main filter
firms.pipeline_intern: Trader: 75-question / 10-minute mental-maths OA with negative marking and a 1-year ban on failure. A '30 questions in 20 minutes about Python code' MCQ test also reported.
firms.pipeline_ft: HackerRank ~12 questions with C++11/14 snippets, ~2 h - 'most people fail at this stage'. Topics: templates/metaprogramming, concurrency design patterns, websockets/socket programming. Then a pair-programming hour with a senior, then onsite with tech managers. Graduate C++ programme take-home: a TCP risk server computing worst hypothetical net position per instrument from a binary order/trade feed.
themes: C++ language quiz rather than algorithms
36-h C++17 TCP risk-server case study with packed binary structs
Mental-maths gate with negative marking
Pair programming with a senior engineer
firms.verdict: The OA is a C++ knowledge test, not a LeetCode test. Failure on the trader maths gate carries a one-year ban.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank of ~12 questions in ~2 hours built around C++11/14 snippets, templates and metaprogramming, concurrency patterns and socket programming. 'Most people fail at this stage.' Then a pair-programming hour and an onsite. Graduate C++ programme adds a TCP risk-server take-home.
roleNotes.trader: 75 mental-maths questions in 10 minutes with negative marking. Failing carries a one-year reapplication ban. A separate Python-code multiple-choice test has also been reported.

firms.name: Two Sigma
firms.langs: Your choice (Python common); C++ for execution/market-data teams.
firms.oa: HackerRank 60-75 min, 2 questions; quant tracks report 3-hour OAs
firms.difficulty: High; DSA rounds consistently described as hard
firms.pipeline_intern: HackerRank OA - intern OAs are LeetCode-easy but share the distinctive stats-to-code theme (piecewise linear interpolation, predict daily temperature by regression).
firms.pipeline_ft: HackerRank 60-75 min -> pair-programming round (implement a binary tree class and debug intentionally incorrect functions in Python) -> three back-to-back technical hours. Nov 2025 report: 'first technical was a LeetCode hard, next two back-to-back also hard - BFS/DFS with math and binary search, 60 min each, pretty intense'. QR adds model design then live coding then a stats round (OLS proofs, Lagrange multipliers).
themes: Signature stats-to-code family: interpolation, online regression, hypothesis tests
LRU/LFU, stream median, matching engine, in-memory DB
Pair-programming debug round
Less C++ internals than HFTs; more design
firms.verdict: The closest thing to a FAANG loop in this list, but with a statistics layer bolted on for quant tracks.

roleNotes.dev: HackerRank (60-75 min, 2 questions), a pair-programming round implementing a binary tree class and debugging intentionally broken functions, then three back-to-back technical hours reported as LeetCode-hard.
roleNotes.researcher: OA with the firm's signature statistics-to-code family: piecewise linear interpolation and extrapolation, online no-intercept regression with a streaming slope, temperature prediction by regression. Quant tracks report 3-hour OAs. Onsite adds model design then live coding then a stats round on OLS proofs and Lagrange multipliers.

firms.name: D. E. Shaw
firms.langs: C++/Java/Python. OOP design in C++ common.
firms.oa: HackerRank ~80 min, 3-4 problems
firms.pipeline_intern: OA: 3 DSA problems in ~80 min (20/20/40 min splits; DP, greedy, bitmask) -> R1 30 min: graph cycle detection in C++ plus a project deep-dive on inheritance and smart pointers -> R2 20 min: design a Banking System class in C++.
firms.pipeline_ft: OA of 4 LeetCode medium-hards -> interviews: 2 LeetCode mediums + a data-structures question -> senior round on OS, DP and databases -> resume grilling. QA/QR track is probability-first with a small data-analysis component.
themes: Largest verified OA pool of the research funds

Code up a queue implementation of a streaming median estimator.

questions.text: System design question regarding stock buying and selling.
Binary search vs hash map: discuss the trade-offs depending on CPU cache behaviour.
questions.note: Cache-awareness asked of an intern - unusual, and worth preparing.

questions.text: Return-rate calculations: simple day-to-day returns; with a dividend; and when two companies merge.
Poker: probability of a royal flush; combinatorial counting, used to test maths and programming together.
Onsite: 2 LeetCode-type interviews with a big focus on runtime analysis, and one system design. LeetCode medium for the first question, hard for the second. No extra questions on fundamentals.
Two-on-one technical interview that started with a simple problem statement and continued with ever-shifting requirements.
questions.note: The evolving-spec pairing session is Quadrature's defining format.

questions.text: Programming task that took 8 hours, followed by a 15-minute HR call about your CV. Also described elsewhere as a take-home Python challenge that everyone has to complete.
Questions on the take-home test about identifying arbitrage opportunities.
Four interviews consisting of algorithmic and implementation questions. No specific questions on finance background.
One LeetCode easy or medium problem on iterators, in a 1-hour technical with an engineer.
Two closely related DP problems in the algorithm round of the on-campus loop.
A dedicated C++ interview on language internals, as one of three campus rounds.
Written exam covering aptitude questions, assembly language, Linux, and C++.
Take-home: 'not expected to finish'. Outside sources permitted, but no LLM use.
questions.note: One of the few explicit no-LLM take-home policies on record, alongside HRT's blanket AI prohibition.

questions.text: Probability and brainteaser type questions, some algorithm questions, generally probed on maths and statistics.
Very open-ended problem-solving questions, each its own mini project with a time constraint, then a very long test.
Write the numbers 2^1000 and 5^1000 in decimal notation, next to each other. How many digits does the resulting number have? (Answer: 1001, since 2^n x 5^n = 10^n)
questions.note: One of only two verbatim TGS questions on record. Dated 2014 - treat with caution.

questions.text: Painted-cube brainteaser: a large painted cube is cut into small cubes - how many have a coloured face?
60-minute screen: one data structure question and one statistics question.
questions.note: This is the only direct evidence that TGS tests coding at all.

questions.text: 'Computer system questions' at the onsite.
Derive the formula for least squares regression and state its assumptions.
Find a Nash equilibrium for a game involving probability.
Write pseudocode for a dynamic programming algorithm for a trading-based problem.
Virtual round plus 3 superday rounds on probability and algorithms, C++ required, plus a 1-hour PhD research talk.

questions.text: Write Python code to output all permutations of the list of integers from 1 to n. Analyse time and memory complexity, then find the optimal solution.
Find the smallest non-negative integer absent from a provided collection of numbers. Discuss set logic, sorting trade-offs and the optimal array search.
Reverse a singly linked list, in the first phone round.
questions.note: Dated, but the only Radix SWE screen question on record.

questions.text: Phone screen (no algorithms at all): inline pros and cons; vector vs list internals; how malloc works and demand paging; how the kernel hands memory to processes; sbrk vs mmap.
questions.note: The single most-cited HRT round. Note there is no coding in it at all.

questions.text: Build a piece of a trading system: write OO code that must be as performance-efficient as possible.
questions.note: Candidate solved it but every test timed out - and was rejected. At HRT, TLE is a fail.

questions.text: Order book: add/cancel/match for one symbol. Then: 'now make cancel O(1)' (hash map of id to intrusive list node).
questions.note: HRT publishes this exercise itself: optimise a naive book builder on real crypto add/delete/modify events, with make measure / profile_functions / check.

questions.text: Intern OA (3 questions): add two binary strings; a diamond-pattern matrix cipher; matrix min-queries with row and column removal (two heaps).
Intern OA (3 questions): O(n) counting problem; word search in a character grid; time-string queries via binary search.
Systems intern phone: 45-minute NO-CODING call on Linux/Unix, C++ pointers and memory, Python/Bash, and tooling.
questions.note: The OA was Codility, 90 minutes inside a 2.5 h window, 3 medium questions, C/C++/Python/Go only. 'Correctness and performance are the most important factors.'

questions.text: OA (2 h 10 min, 3 questions): remove comments from C++ source; palindrome permutation; determine whether a chemical equation is balanced. The third had 10+ edge cases and was the hardest.
Roll a die 100 times and flip a coin 400 times: what is P(dice sum > number of heads)? Exact DP expected - Monte Carlo was criticised.
questions.note: A clean illustration of HRT's preference for exact computation over simulation.

questions.text: Two threads each increment a shared counter 1,000,000 times; the final value is less than 2,000,000. Why, and how do you fix it?

You have 4 GB of RAM and allocate an 8 GB buffer - is that possible, and how is it read? Follow-ups on virtual vs physical memory, thread vs process, IPC and named pipes, vtables, map vs unordered_map, hashtable collisions and resizing, the GIL, TCP vs UDP.
questions.srcname: Verbatim dump of ~60 HRT Glassdoor items

questions.text: Design a system to route packets between one hub and many node servers.

Onsite data-science round: pandas and prediction tasks. SQL joins with CTEs. 'Pandas question - expected if it's on your resume.'
25 bunnies, 5 lanes, no timer - how many races to find the fastest three? (Answer: 7.) HRT warns candidates to say if they have seen it before.
Eulerian-path feasibility from odd-degree vertex counts (0/2/4 odd vertices, with an add-one-edge variant).
questions.note: Matches LeetCode 'Add Edges to Make Degrees of All Nodes Even', HRT-tagged at 97% frequency.

questions.text: QR intern: NO online assessment. Three rounds - HR call, then a round with coding plus a trading-strategy / game-theory problem, then a further round.
Quant summer intern OA: 3 questions in a 105-minute window on Codility. Reported problems: validate that a string has all a's before all b's; a tree-cost DP.

Coding problems around LeetCode medium/hard with important C++ concepts: string manipulation, reference counting, I/O, move semantics. Core-dev roles add kernel, concurrency and CPU-architecture questions.
Can you create a linked list? Implement it. Then: write a function to swap the positions of two given nodes. In C++.
Take-home order-book exercise used for SWE hires - message formats recovered in a public artifact.
2025 SRE/infra code round: four Codility-style problems solved in Python, including smallest missing positive integer (N up to 1e5, values +/-1e6, O(N) required).
In-person technical round on C, pointers and arrays, plus implementing a hash map from scratch.
questions.note: Dated but consistent with later 'implement a container from scratch' reports.

questions.text: R2 fundamentals round: calculate the sum and prefix sum of n elements using p threads; analyse inefficient C++ for branch prediction; sort an extremely large array with limited RAM.
HackerRank 1 hour in 3 sections: 3 DSA problems (Codeforces 1600-1800 level), probability/maths, and C++/Python OOP plus computer architecture.

questions.text: Interview on TLB and huge pages, RISC vs CISC, shared vs static libraries, syscalls at the assembly level, and pipelining/branch prediction.
questions.srcname: GeeksforGeeks / question bank with source URLs

questions.text: MCQ OA plus 4 coding problems: SQL, find the bug in this Python, parsing, and an algorithm question.
R1: LeetCode medium/hard plus probability puzzles plus pandas details.

Quant Trading Analyst: Codility, 5 questions / 75 minutes, 'mostly on the lower end of LeetCode Medium (if not easies)'. Candidate finished in ~37 minutes, then was rejected after a brainteaser phone round with no feedback.
C++ core/HFT: 4 back-to-back rounds on multithreading and concurrency. Thread-safe LRU cache. TCP vs UDP and why market data uses UDP. Design order routing with partial fills and retries.
Phone brainteasers, e.g. clock-hand angles; post-trade onsite described as 'brain teasers 4 hours straight'.
Linux command-line challenge; implement unordered_map from scratch; a LeetCode-hard OA with no visible tests for senior roles.
C++-mandatory HackerRank OA, 90-120 min: an as-of join on CSV rows.

questions.text: OA problem 'Disaster Recovery' - a union-find problem.
Loop of up to 10+ C++/OS/concurrency rounds: malloc vs new, std::copy vs memcpy.
1-hour technical video screen: implement a well-known data structure. Then a 5-hour virtual onsite of 4 technical DS&A interviews plus a CTO chat.
questions.note: Also reported: C pointer and struct minutiae.

questions.text: Quant rounds are rapid fire at roughly 30 seconds per question: dice expected values, tournament probabilities, Fermi estimates.

'Giving Tree of Errors': input pairs (A,B)(B,C)(A,D). Build a binary tree and print the S-expression (A(B(C))(D)) with children lexicographically ordered. Error codes: E1 invalid input, E2 duplicate pair, E3 more than 2 children, E4 multiple roots, E5 cycle.
questions.date: 2020, re-confirmed 2022 and again in a 2026 OA guide
questions.note: Reported unchanged across at least three cycles. The error-code spec is the real difficulty, not the tree.

questions.text: 'Numbers Station' message decoder: a stream of (sequence id, char or '-'); a message is the chars between two hyphens. Handle out-of-order samples, emit only the latest completed message, and handle the 'two words complete simultaneously' rule.
Days between two dates without using Date objects, with leap-year edge cases. Paired with a graph problem in a 2-hour OA.
questions.note: C++ solution repo: github.com/bencimp/days-between

questions.text: Future-price / dividend adjustment: given stock price S and dividends (amount, day), the price from that day onward is reduced additively. Later formalised as a FuturePricingEngine with update-dividend-by-id and query(day).

'Lion/Elephant Competition': the constructor takes your animals (name, size) plus a private enter/exit schedule; rivals arrive via entered(time,size) and left(time,size); getBiggest(currentTime) returns your animals at least as tall as the tallest rival present.
Supermarket checkout tracker: customers enter and exit, switch lines, and modify baskets; notify on exit. 2-hour OA.
questions.note: Candidate passed 95% of tests.

questions.text: System design (verbal, intern onsite): 'You are a trader in Amsterdam, the exchange is in Frankfurt - design the system.' Pushed iteratively toward automation and co-location.
questions.note: Appears at intern, graduate and final-round level. If you prepare one Optiver design answer, prepare this one.

questions.text: Order-book simulation: process buys and sells; a buy matches the lowest sell at or below its price, a sell matches the highest buy at or above its price. Output the sum of transaction prices.
'Trading sequences': count the distinct sequences from k shares to n shares in at most m one-share buy/sell transactions, with holdings never negative.
LogServer: recordLog(id, ts), GetLogs() returning at most m latest ids from the last hour in ascending ts, and GetLogCount().

'Worst Trade Reporter': a stream of Trade(TradeID, InstrumentID, Buy/Sell, Price, Volume) plus price updates. Query the worst loss-per-lot trade per instrument, ties broken by latest, else 'NO BAD TRADES'.
'Truck Positions': S client truck to subscribe, U truck dx dy to move, R client to return the current position plus the delta since the last request. Starter classes supplied; 2-hour OA.
questions.note: Candidate called it 'impossible for 2 hours'.

questions.text: Write your own vector; CPU cache and TLB; multithreading with notify_all; memory-leak detection and avoidance; circular-buffer queue.
Speed of light: what is the round-trip time for a packet between Amsterdam and Singapore?

Coding round (~60 min, two engineers observing): parse, build and traverse a graph, with requirements escalating throughout. Written feedback cited 'iteration speed below expectations' and 'limited ability to adapt as requirements became more complex'.
questions.srcname: First-hand repo including the actual recruiter feedback
questions.note: The single most useful document in this database for understanding how Optiver grades.

questions.text: QT/QR intern OA: 80 arithmetic questions in 8 minutes (+1/-1 scoring), sequence and pattern games, 10 probability questions at 90 seconds each, and a personality test. No coding.
Onsite: implement a matching engine from skeleton code and pass the unit tests - add order, delete order, partial fills, multi-level sweeps. Reported as 'always the same question'.
questions.note: A Senior Java Dev in India passed 44 tests in a 2.5-hour station and was still rejected for not following the prescribed approach.

questions.text: OA: knight minimum path with a fixed bishop at (bi,bj); the knight may never land on a square the bishop attacks. BFS.
OA: a stack with push/pop/peek, range increment on the first i elements, and O(1) sum(). (LeetCode 1381 plus a sum operation.)
questions.note: The lazy-increment fix is required to avoid TLE. This family recurs across intern and new-grad OAs.

questions.text: Group code review: a C++ ResourceManager / order-processing snippet using threads. Find the bugs, optimise it, and discuss OS scheduling.
questions.note: A group code-review round is unusual - IMC swaps deep C++ trivia for this at intern level.

questions.text: 90-minute technical: 30 minutes discussing the optimal order-book approach, then 60 minutes coding it.
MEX problem: sort, then greedily assign 0,1,2,... (Q1 of 7; Q2-Q6 were MCQ.)
Seat-assignment queue: requests [1,3,3,2,2] map to [1,3,4,2,5]. Union-find or ordered-set solutions.

How are smart pointers implemented (control block, atomic refcount, destructor across threads)? Vtable memory layout under multiple inheritance, and virtual destructors. Also false sharing, move constructors, and CPU caches.

Differences between list, set, map and unordered_map; 'sort from fastest to slowest: CPU cache, main memory, heap allocation, addition, disk'; what happens when you type wikipedia.org. Also: 'Is multithreading always faster than single-threading?'

A robot on a table moves left or right with given probabilities, starting x cm from the edge - expected number of moves to fall off. Plus dice/cards probability, a market-making game, and video questions defining eigenvalues, survivor bias and conditional probability.
Superday: implement std::vector from scratch. Plus a system-design round and a maths-focused round.
questions.note: The canonical SIG C++ question.

questions.text: Technical phone screen: perform joins, merges and aggregates in numpy/pandas.
Coding round: write the code, explain it, and justify your data structure and complexity. A separate design round requires an extensible SOLID design.
questions.note: Insider advice from another Blind post: know 'when and where to use data structures'; you do not need the single optimal solution.

questions.text: Stage 1 maths entrance exam: 14 questions in 20 minutes - expectations of infinite streams, bet EV vs cost, brainteasers. Then an HR-led round with 5 probability questions. NO coding at any stage.
questions.note: Candidate was rejected with a recorded probability rating of 2 - the failure was maths, not code.

questions.text: 72-hour take-home order matching engine in C++. stdin commands: BUY|SELL <GFD|IOC> <price> <qty> <orderId>, MODIFY, CANCEL, PRINT. GFD rests; IOC fills-or-cancels; price-time priority; print TRADE lines and the book on PRINT.
questions.srcname: Public repo with the spec and 4 sample inputs
questions.note: Graded on hidden tests with a 2-second limit. One candidate passed 29/30 and failed the last case on std::cin throughput.

questions.text: C++ SWE intern OA (80 min, 3 problems): (1) simplified market-order tracking - process buy/sell orders and cancels, maintain bid/offer, recompute the best quote after each event; (2) data throttling / rate limiter - publish items subject to size and count caps per sliding window, dropping excess.

Refactor a buggy C++ object pool: races, double-free, ABA, leaks. Implement borrow() with timeout/blocking, returnObject(), and an RAII handle (movable, non-copyable), with FIFO fairness and safe shutdown. Deliver C++17 plus multithreaded unit tests.

Junior QR OA: 3 LeetCode-mediums (one simulation-based greedy, one standard greedy, one simple memoisation/pre-computation), C++ or Python, solve any two. Explicitly graded on cleanliness and readability.
questions.note: Rejection wording: 'We decided to proceed with candidates who demonstrated even stronger proficiency in probability and statistics, as well as strong coding skills.'

questions.text: Codility OA, 3 questions / 150 minutes: bank transfers; letter arrangement with lexicographic ordering; string manipulation with constraints. Partial credit awarded; more points if at least one of the three is written in C++.

Tetris engine take-home (4-page PDF spec): simplified Tetris on a 10-wide grid with pieces Q, Z, S, T, I, L, J and a column offset (e.g. Q0,I4,L8). Pieces drop until they rest, full rows clear and rows above drop. Input is one comma-separated piece sequence per line; output the resulting stack height per line.
questions.srcname: Public repo with the original PDF and 20 test lines
questions.note: Extended live at the onsite - you build on your own take-home in front of the interviewer.

questions.text: Write pseudocode to serialise a struct to a binary file. How do you handle endianness?
Codility OA (3/150): bulb-switcher toggle simulation; max even sum choosing K elements; minimum-length subarray containing all distinct elements.

Graduate C++ programme take-home: a 'Risk server' - a TCP server computing the worst hypothetical net position per instrument from a binary order/trade feed, with packed binary structs. 36-hour window.

HackerRank ~12 questions (more than half programming) with C++11/14 snippets, ~2 hours: templates and metaprogramming, concurrency design patterns, websockets and socket programming. 'Most people fail at this stage.'
questions.note: This is a C++ knowledge test, not a LeetCode test.

OA: piecewise linear interpolation and extrapolation (n, q up to 2e5); predict daily temperature by regression; online no-intercept linear regression with a streaming slope.
questions.note: The signature Two Sigma family: statistics translated into code, not LeetCode. If you prepare one thing for Two Sigma, prepare this.

questions.text: Hybrid 3-hour HackerRank: 1 coding question (LeetCode medium-hard) plus 2 regression problems - run a regression on a provided dataset using scikit-learn.

Three rounds of technical interviews including one on model design (predicting rent prices in Manhattan), followed by live coding and a stats round covering proofs of OLS, optimisation and Lagrange multipliers.
Pair-programming round in Python: implement a binary tree class and debug intentionally incorrect functions.

Technical screens: an in-memory limit-order matcher with price-time priority; an in-memory relational DB supporting CREATE/INSERT/SELECT WHERE; an RPN calculator with Token/Operand/Operator plus a factory pattern.
OA: decode a string encoded using a specific algorithm - explicitly not a standard LeetCode problem. 60-75 min, 2 questions.
OA: 3 DSA problems in ~80 minutes with 20/20/40 minute splits - DP, greedy, and bitmask.

OA: 4 LeetCode medium-hards. Interviews: 2 LeetCode mediums plus a data-structures question; a senior round on OS, DP and databases; then resume grilling.

Two-week take-home project asking you to complete almost a whole research pipeline.

HackerRank, 45 minutes, 5 questions: 2 SQL and 3 Python.

Cubist multi-part take-home with components such as a Thinknum review, a TreasuryDirect scrape, and portfolio P&L. Interview covers classifier metrics, live-vs-backtest failure diagnosis, and Wald vs Bayesian confidence intervals.
TLE-trap problems: compute percentiles without NumPy; frequency sort; divisor counting; Advantage Shuffle.

~1-hour HackerRank, easy-to-medium but skewed toward implementation rather than clever tricks: e.g. parse a string of commands and execute them in order, or simulate a series of transactions between bank accounts.
Debug a broken vector implementation; count constructor calls in a given snippet; review a thread-safe queue benchmark. Plus OS fundamentals.

HackerRank OA: three LeetCode-medium problems. Verified new-grad OA titles include 'Keep Them Apart' and 'Array Nullification'.
QR intern: Codility 60 minutes, then a separate 50-minute CSV data exam.

questions.note: Rejection feedback: 'strong technically but question marks over approach and communication style - jumped into answers before thinking, which led to sub-optimal solutions.'

syllabus.why: Akuna's rate limiter, Optiver's LogServer last-hour window, HRT's sliding-window maximum. The 'window' framing is everywhere because trading data is a stream.

syllabus.why: HRT time-string queries, Rokos Codility, Citadel 'Get Max Throughput' (binary search on the bottleneck), Two Sigma hard rounds.

syllabus.evidence: IMC 'always the same question'; HRT's own public workshop; Akuna 72-h take-home; Citadel Securities NBBO.

syllabus.why: Citadel tags Merge Intervals, Employee Free Time, Meeting Rooms II and Meeting Scheduler. Akuna's weighted interval scheduling.

syllabus.why: Consistently under-prepared. Citadel Securities' 2-hour obfuscated-C++ round, Squarepoint's broken vector, Akuna's buggy object pool, IMC's group code review, G-Research's performance-from-logs.

works.d: The dominant format is one problem extended two or three times. Practise the second and third step: bound the cache, make cancel O(1), make it thread-safe, handle the new rule.
works.ev: Jane Street official Memo problem; HRT order book; Optiver escalating graph round; Quadrature shifting requirements.

doesnt.d: Officially counterproductive: 'We don't award bonus points for using a functional language like OCaml. Please don't use OCaml just because you think it will make us happy.'
doesnt.ev: Jane Street official SWE interview prep page.

doesnt.d: Traders need probability; developers and researchers need working code. Collecting puzzles is the classic misallocation for dev candidates.
doesnt.ev: QuantNet hiring manager: many strong-maths PhDs rejected for weak software engineering background.

A Citadel Securities senior SWE was rejected for missing self-loops in the currency-graph problem. A Jane Street candidate fixed an edge case live and was still rejected.

failures.d: 'I probably spent too much time explaining and didn't have enough time to finish the code.' Multi-step questions require you to reach the final step.

failures.d: Quadrature's two-on-one runs on ever-shifting requirements; Optiver's feedback cited 'limited ability to adapt as requirements became more complex'.
failures.ev: Blind Quadrature onsite; Optiver principal-SWE feedback.

failures.ev: HRT first-hand phone screen; Citadel Securities Blind reports.

failures.ev: Mustard Systems take-home feedback; Tibra QTD feedback.

failures.d: Out-of-sample discipline is the thing take-home reviewers look for. A Sharpe of 3.0 in-sample presented without caveat reads as a red flag, not a result.
failures.ev: Take-home grading rubric synthesis; XTX 'model that failed in production' question.

budgets.weeks: 8-12 weeks (experienced: ~30 days at 2-3 h/day if your DSA is current)

budgets.note: Experienced loops have fewer OAs and stricter holistic judging. Grinding volume is low-yield; C++ depth, concurrency, debugging and ownership stories are what actually get tested.

budgets.split: 40% probability/statistics, 30% Python + numpy/pandas, 30% timed DSA at LeetCode-medium
budgets.note: Intern QR keeps a data/regression OA plus a DSA live round, but the multi-week take-homes appear only at full-time level.

budgets.note: Optiver, SIG and IMC do not test coding for trader interns at all. Every first-hand trader rejection here was attributed to probability or maths.

drills.t: Limit order book with O(1) cancel
