BUY/SELL with GFD and IOC semantics, MODIFY, CANCEL, PRINT. Partial fills and multi-level sweeps. Watch input throughput.
Hash map plus doubly-linked list, O(1) get and put. Jane Street's official Memo question ends here.
Growth policy, iterator invalidation, move semantics; then buckets, collisions and rehashing.
Atomics, memory ordering, and alignas(64) to avoid false sharing.
Two heaps; then rolling max, mean and mode over a sliding window.
Two Sigma's signature family. Implement OLS with a streaming slope update and no intercept.

drills.t: A rate limiter / throttler over a sliding window
drills.d: Size and count caps per window, dropping excess. Akuna asks this directly; Optiver's LogServer is the same shape.

drills.t: A small game or state machine from a loose spec
drills.d: Tetris, Connect Four on an infinite board, a stack machine, a supermarket checkout. Practise clarifying an underspecified prompt, then extending your own design twice.

stats.sub: The interview gate and the substrate for everything after it. Nothing later in this syllabus is safe to attempt before this module is automatic.

items.t: Conditional probability, Bayes, law of total probability
items.know: Bayes in odds form as well as ratio form. Law of total probability and total expectation, E[X] = E[E[X|Y]], as your default decomposition tool. Independence versus conditional independence, and why the second does not imply the first.
items.why: This is the single most-tested topic across every trader and researcher loop in the database. Citadel Securities' captured OA includes a rigged-dice Bayes question verbatim; SIG's 14-question entrance exam and Five Rings' 30-second rapid-fire rounds are built almost entirely on it.
items.check: You can do a three-step Bayes update in your head, in odds form, without writing the denominator.

items.know: Linearity of expectation without independence. Var(aX+bY) with covariance. Law of total variance, Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var(E[X|Y]). Conditional expectation as a projection.
items.why: Linearity of expectation without independence is the trick behind most 'expected number of...' interview questions, and law of total variance is how you decompose strategy PnL into signal and noise components.
items.check: You can compute the expected number of fixed points in a random permutation in one line, using indicators and no combinatorics.

items.t: The distributions that actually arise, and why
items.know: Bernoulli/binomial, Poisson, exponential, normal, lognormal, uniform. For each: the generating mechanism, the memorylessness or lack of it, and the limiting relationships between them. Poisson process specifically: superposition, thinning, conditional uniformity of arrival times, and interarrival exponentiality.
items.why: Order flow is modelled as a point process, so Poisson structure is the working vocabulary of market microstructure. Citadel Securities' captured OA contains two Poisson questions: conditional uniformity of a single arrival, and the merged rate of two superposed processes.
items.check: Given 'exactly one arrival occurred in [0,T]', you immediately know its location is uniform, and can say why without computing.

items.know: Distribution of the max and min of n i.i.d. draws. Expected value of the k-th order statistic for the uniform case. Expected maximum growth rate for common tails.
items.why: Best-of-N quotes, worst-case fills, and the expected best price across venues are all order statistics. Also the honest way to think about why the best-looking backtest out of 200 is not evidence.
items.check: You can derive E[max of n uniforms] = n/(n+1) from the CDF in under a minute.

items.know: MGF as a sum-of-independents tool and a moment extractor. Why the lognormal has no MGF. Cumulants and their additivity.
items.why: The clean route to sums of independent random variables and to proving CLT-type results. Appears in the harder written tests such as G-Research's triage round.
items.check: You can get the variance of a compound Poisson sum by differentiating the MGF twice, without looking anything up.

items.know: Law of large numbers versus central limit theorem, and what each does and does not promise. Chebyshev. The delta method. Slutsky. Rate of convergence, and why root-n is the number that governs your career.
items.why: Every Sharpe ratio, every t-statistic and every sample size decision is a root-n argument. The delta method is how you get the standard error of a ratio such as a Sharpe estimate.
items.check: You can state, from memory, why the standard error of an estimated Sharpe ratio is approximately sqrt((1+S^2/2)/T).

stats.sub: Where 'expected time until' questions come from, and the mathematics behind gambler's-ruin and market-making intuition.

items.know: Transition matrices, communicating classes, stationary distributions. First-passage and absorption times set up by first-step analysis: E[T_i] = 1 + sum_j p_ij E[T_j]. Solve the linear system, do not simulate.
items.why: The engine behind the entire 'expected number of rolls until you see HH / 3,4,5 consecutively' family, which Jane Street, Citadel Securities and SIG all ask. Squarepoint tests Markov chains explicitly in later rounds.
items.check: You can set up and solve 'expected flips until HH' in under three minutes on paper, and explain why it differs from HT.

items.know: Recurrence in one and two dimensions versus transience in three. Hitting probabilities and gambler's ruin with fair and unfair coins. The reflection principle. Expected maximum drawdown of a random walk.
items.why: Gambler's ruin is the mathematical statement of position sizing and risk of ruin. The reflection principle answers a surprising number of path-dependent interview questions in one line.
items.check: You can compute the probability of reaching +a before -b for a biased walk without re-deriving the whole recursion.

items.know: The definition, and the three conditions under which optional stopping applies. Constructing a martingale from a game to price it. Wald's identity.
items.why: Optional stopping turns many 'what is this game worth' questions into a single line, which is exactly what strong trader candidates do and weak ones grind through by recursion. Jane Street's betting-game rounds reward this directly.
items.check: Given a stopping-time question, your first instinct is to look for the martingale rather than to set up a recursion.

items.know: Independent Gaussian increments, scaling, quadratic variation, non-differentiability. Reflection principle for Brownian motion, hitting times.
items.why: The continuous-time limit that underlies pricing intuition. Needed at a properties level even for statistical-arbitrage roles that never touch Ito calculus.
items.check: You can say what the quadratic variation of Brownian motion over [0,T] equals, and why that fact makes ordinary calculus fail.

stats.sub: The part of a statistics degree that survives contact with a research desk. Much of the rest does not.

items.know: Maximum likelihood: write the likelihood, take logs, differentiate. Method of moments. Bias, variance, mean squared error, and the decomposition MSE = bias^2 + variance. Consistency versus unbiasedness, and why you often prefer a biased estimator.
items.why: The bias-variance decomposition is the intellectual core of why shrinkage and regularisation work, which is the daily reality of return prediction. Two Sigma tests OLS proofs directly; Citadel Securities' OA asks which regulariser produces sparse coefficients.
items.check: You can derive the MLE for the variance of a normal sample and say precisely why it is biased and by how much.

items.know: Standard error of a mean, a difference, a proportion, a correlation, a regression coefficient. Confidence intervals and their correct interpretation. When the normal approximation fails.
items.why: Nearly every research claim is 'this number is bigger than its standard error'. Getting the standard error wrong is the most common way to be confidently wrong on a desk.
items.check: You can state the standard error of a sample correlation and explain why it is not symmetric, motivating Fisher's z transform.

items.know: t-tests and their assumptions. p-values and what they are not. Type I and II error, power, and why power is the neglected half. The distinction between statistical and economic significance.
items.why: Standard, but the honest version matters: a signal significant at p=0.05 that does not survive transaction costs is worthless, and saying so is a hiring signal.
items.check: You can explain to a non-statistician why a p-value is not the probability the hypothesis is true.

items.t: Multiple testing and the research process
items.know: Family-wise error rate, Bonferroni, and false discovery rate with Benjamini-Hochberg. The garden of forking paths. Why testing 200 signals at p=0.05 guarantees roughly 10 false discoveries.
items.why: Signal research IS multiple testing. This is the single most important statistical idea separating a researcher who will produce durable alpha from one who will produce overfit noise, and it is the substance behind XTX's question about a model that failed in production.
items.check: You can compute how many of your 'discoveries' are expected to be false given the number of tests and your threshold, and adjust the threshold accordingly.

items.know: Non-parametric and block bootstrap. Permutation tests for the null of no relationship. Why the block variant is mandatory for autocorrelated financial data.
items.why: Financial returns violate nearly every parametric assumption. Resampling gives you honest intervals without pretending returns are normal and independent, and the block variant is the version that respects autocorrelation.
items.check: You know why an ordinary i.i.d. bootstrap on daily returns understates uncertainty, and what block length to choose.

items.t: Bayesian reasoning as a working tool
items.know: Conjugate priors for the normal and beta-binomial cases. Shrinkage as the posterior mean. Credible versus confidence intervals.
items.why: Shrinking a noisy estimate toward a prior is what you actually do with sparse data on a desk. Point72's Cubist asks about Wald versus Bayesian intervals directly.
items.check: You can explain James-Stein shrinkage in one sentence and say why it beats the sample mean.

stats.sub: The workhorse. A QR who genuinely understands regression outperforms one who knows ten models superficially.

items.know: Derive the normal equations by calculus. Derive the same result as an orthogonal projection onto the column space. Know the closed form beta = (X'X)^-1 X'y and why you never compute it that way numerically.
items.why: Radix asks you to derive least squares and state its assumptions. Two Sigma asks for OLS proofs. The projection view is what makes residualisation, factor neutralisation and partialling-out obvious rather than mysterious.
items.check: You can derive the normal equations both ways in under ten minutes, and explain what the hat matrix does geometrically.

items.know: The assumptions individually, what each buys you, and the specific consequence when each fails. Unbiasedness versus efficiency. Why normality is not needed for unbiasedness.
items.why: Knowing which assumption is violated and what it costs is the difference between a diagnosis and a shrug. Interviewers escalate here reliably.
items.check: For each of the five assumptions you can name the failure mode and its consequence for coefficients versus standard errors.

items.t: Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, and robust standard errors
items.know: White/Huber-Eicker robust standard errors. Newey-West HAC for autocorrelated errors. Clustered standard errors when observations group by time or asset.
items.why: This is not a footnote in finance, it is the main event. Naive OLS standard errors on overlapping or autocorrelated financial data are wrong by large factors, and reporting them uncorrected is a visible error in a take-home.
items.check: You can say why overlapping-window returns inflate t-statistics and which correction fixes it.

items.know: The direction and magnitude of omitted variable bias. Variance inflation. Why collinearity harms interpretation without harming prediction.
items.why: Factor models are collinear by construction. Knowing that collinearity destabilises coefficients but not fitted values keeps you from solving the wrong problem.
items.check: Given a fitted model and a named omitted variable, you can state the sign of the bias.

items.t: R-squared and its irrelevance to return prediction
items.know: R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and the fact that a genuinely valuable return-prediction model typically has R-squared in the low single digits of a percent. Information coefficient as the metric that is actually used.
items.why: A candidate who dismisses a model because R-squared is 0.01 reveals they have never worked with returns. The corresponding signal is knowing that an IC of 0.03 can be a real, tradeable edge.
items.check: You can convert between an information coefficient and an approximate Sharpe ratio using the fundamental law of active management.

items.know: Ridge as shrinkage with a closed form and a bias-variance interpretation. LASSO as a sparsity-inducing L1 penalty, and geometrically why the corner solution zeroes coefficients. Elastic net. Selecting the penalty by cross-validation.
items.why: Citadel Securities' captured OA asks which regulariser gives sparse coefficients. Millennium asks LASSO versus ridge directly. Beyond interviews, shrinkage is the correct default when predictors are many and signal is weak, which is always.
items.check: You can draw the L1 and L2 constraint regions and explain from the picture why L1 produces exact zeros.

items.know: WLS when variance is known up to a scale. GLS with a general covariance. The connection to robust standard errors.
items.why: Volatility varies enormously across assets and regimes; weighting by inverse variance is how you stop the noisiest names dominating a fit.
items.check: You can say when WLS strictly beats OLS and what you need to know to use it.

items.know: The logit link, maximum likelihood fitting, coefficient interpretation as log-odds. Precision, recall, ROC-AUC, and why accuracy is meaningless under class imbalance.
items.why: Direction-of-move prediction is a classification problem, and Point72's Cubist asks about classifier metrics explicitly.
items.check: You can explain why a 99% accurate model can be useless, using a concrete class-imbalance example.

stats.t: Time series and the structure of financial data
stats.sub: Where general statistics stops being sufficient and finance becomes its own discipline.

items.know: Weak versus strict stationarity. Random walks versus mean-reverting series. Augmented Dickey-Fuller and its low power. Differencing and what it costs.
items.why: Prices are non-stationary, returns are approximately stationary. Regressing one price on another produces spurious results, which is the classic novice error in a take-home.
items.check: You can explain the spurious regression problem and demonstrate it in five lines of simulation.

items.t: Autocorrelation structure: ACF, PACF, AR, MA, ARMA
items.know: Reading ACF and PACF to identify order. AR and MA as models for short-horizon dependence. Why return autocorrelation is near zero but absolute-return autocorrelation is strongly positive.
items.why: The near-zero autocorrelation of returns alongside strong autocorrelation of volatility is the central stylised fact of financial data, and it drives the split between direction models and risk models.
items.check: You can sketch, from memory, the ACF of daily returns versus the ACF of squared daily returns.

items.know: Exponentially weighted moving average variance as the practical baseline. GARCH(1,1), its persistence parameter, and volatility clustering. Realised volatility from high-frequency data.
items.why: Position sizing is inverse to forecast volatility, so a volatility model is upstream of every risk decision. EWMA is often good enough, and knowing that is itself a signal.
items.check: You can implement EWMA variance in two lines and explain what the decay parameter means in terms of an effective lookback.

items.know: Cointegration as a stationary linear combination of non-stationary series. Engle-Granger two-step, Johansen for multiple series. Half-life of mean reversion from an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fit.
items.why: This is the mathematical basis of pairs trading and statistical arbitrage. If you are interviewing for stat-arb research, expect to be asked how you would identify and trade a cointegrated pair.
items.check: You can estimate the half-life of a mean-reverting spread and explain how it sets your holding period.

items.know: Look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, point-in-time data versus restated data, and the subtle case of using a full-sample scaler before splitting.
items.why: These are how backtests lie. Every take-home reviewer is looking for them, and finding one in your own work before they do is the strongest possible signal.
items.check: You can list three ways look-ahead bias enters a pipeline and how you would test for each.

stats.sub: What happens when you have more assets than you have history, which is the normal condition.

items.know: Why the sample covariance matrix is badly conditioned and nearly singular when the number of assets approaches the number of observations. Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage toward a structured target.
items.why: Portfolio optimisation inverts the covariance matrix, so a badly estimated one produces extreme, unstable weights. This is the practical reason naive mean-variance optimisation fails.
items.check: You can say what happens to the smallest eigenvalues as the asset count approaches the sample size, and why that wrecks an optimiser.

items.know: PCA as an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix. Interpreting the leading eigenvector as a market factor. Explained variance. The link to singular value decomposition.
items.why: The first principal component of an equity cross-section is essentially the market. Factor neutralisation, risk decomposition and dimension reduction all run through this.
items.check: You can compute PCA from a covariance matrix by hand for a two-asset case and interpret both components.

items.know: The Marchenko-Pastur distribution as the eigenvalue spectrum of pure noise. Distinguishing signal eigenvalues from the noise bulk.
items.why: It gives you a principled answer to 'how many factors are real', instead of picking a number because the scree plot looked bent there.
items.check: You can state what the noise bulk edge depends on and why it widens as you add assets.

items.know: Cross-sectional versus time-series factor models. Alpha and beta decomposition. Risk model versus alpha model, and why they must be kept separate.
items.why: The organising framework of institutional quant investing. G-Research officially recommends the first four chapters of Grinold and Kahn, which is exactly this material.
items.check: You can explain why you neutralise a signal against known factors before evaluating it.

items.know: Sharpe and its standard error. Information ratio, information coefficient, and the fundamental law of active management. Maximum drawdown. Turnover and transaction costs. Deflated Sharpe under multiple testing.
items.why: You will be asked to evaluate a strategy, and 'the Sharpe is 3.0' without a standard error, a cost assumption or a trials count is the answer that fails take-homes.
items.check: Given a Sharpe ratio and a sample length, you can say whether it is statistically distinguishable from zero.

stats.sub: Conditional module. Load this only if you are targeting options market makers. For pure statistical-arbitrage research it is over-preparation, and the depth below is the ceiling, not the floor.

items.t: Ito's lemma and the Black-Scholes derivation
items.know: Ito's lemma applied to a function of a geometric Brownian motion. The replicating-portfolio derivation of Black-Scholes. Risk-neutral pricing as a change of measure, at the level of intuition rather than measure theory.
items.why: Optiver, IMC, SIG, Akuna, Jane Street and Da Vinci all trade options and ask about pricing. Optiver has asked candidates to derive Black-Scholes and then re-derive it via a binomial tree.
items.check: You can derive Black-Scholes from a binomial tree in the limit and explain what risk-neutral pricing does and does not claim.

items.t: The Greeks and what traders actually use
items.know: Delta, gamma, vega, theta, and their signs and rough magnitudes. Delta hedging and the gamma-theta trade-off. Put-call parity as a no-arbitrage identity.
items.why: Market makers manage a Greek book, so the questions are practical: given a delta of 0.5 and a one-cent move in the underlying, what happens to the option price. Put-call parity is the most-asked derivatives identity in trader interviews.
items.check: You can state put-call parity from memory and use it to price a synthetic position instantly.

items.know: Implied volatility as the inverted price. The smile and skew, and their economic explanation. Term structure. Realised versus implied volatility.
items.why: The volatility surface is the object an options desk trades, and 'why is there a skew' is a standard question.
items.check: You can explain the equity skew in terms of both crash risk and leverage, and say why it is not present in every asset class.

code.sub: Not syntax. The subset of the language that makes research code correct and fast enough to be trusted.

items.know: Comprehensions, generators and laziness, itertools, collections (defaultdict, Counter, deque), unpacking, sorting with keys, context managers, dataclasses. Mutable default arguments and other standard traps.
items.why: Akuna grades OA submissions explicitly on cleanliness and readability; Optiver progressed a 77.8% submission over a 90% one. Idiomatic code is scored, not merely tolerated.
items.check: You can write a generator pipeline over a large file that never loads it into memory.

items.know: Writing tests as you go. Assertions on shapes and invariants. Reasoning about edge cases before running. Debugging with pdb rather than print statements.
items.why: The most common documented rejection reason across this research is a missed edge case, not a missed algorithm. Jane Street does not let you run your code at all.
items.check: You can write a function and enumerate its edge cases before executing it once.

items.know: Why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Catastrophic cancellation. Relative versus absolute tolerance. Accumulation error in long sums, and why a naive running variance is unstable.
items.why: The naive one-pass variance formula loses precision catastrophically on real data. Knowing Welford's algorithm is a genuine differentiator in a numerical coding round.
items.check: You can state why sum(x^2)/n - mean^2 is a bad variance formula and write the stable alternative.

code.sub: The skill that separates researchers who iterate in minutes from ones who iterate in hours.

items.know: Broadcasting rules in full. dtype and memory implications. Views versus copies, and when an operation silently copies. C versus Fortran memory order and why it changes speed.
items.why: XTX reportedly probes numpy broadcasting internals and memory layout for research candidates. More practically, a researcher who writes Python loops over a million rows cannot do the job.
items.check: Given two arrays of shapes (1000,1) and (50,), you can predict the result shape and whether it allocates.

items.know: Replacing loops with array expressions. np.where, cumsum, diff, einsum for the cases that need it. Sliding windows via stride tricks or convolution. Knowing when vectorising harms readability enough not to.
items.why: This is the day job. It is also why Point72 sets TLE-trap problems such as computing percentiles without NumPy.
items.check: You can compute a rolling z-score over a long series without a Python-level loop.

items.know: solve rather than inv. Least squares via QR or SVD rather than the normal equations. Condition number and what it predicts. eig versus eigh for symmetric matrices.
items.why: Computing (X'X)^-1 X'y directly squares the condition number and loses roughly half your precision. Using lstsq or QR instead is the mark of someone who has done numerical work.
items.check: You can explain why np.linalg.lstsq is preferable to inverting X'X, in terms of condition number.

code.sub: Where research time is actually spent, and the specific source of a documented rejection.

items.know: Indexing with loc and iloc, boolean masks, groupby with transform and agg and apply, merge and join semantics, pivot and melt, MultiIndex. Method chaining.
items.why: SIG's phone screen for trading-systems roles is joins, merges and aggregates in pandas. Millennium's QR OA includes two pandas problems.
items.check: You can compute a within-group demeaned column with groupby transform, in one chained expression.

items.know: DatetimeIndex, resample, rolling and expanding windows, shift and lag, and merge_asof for aligning irregular timestamps.
items.why: merge_asof is the operation for joining trades to prevailing quotes, which is the fundamental tick-data manipulation. Headlands' OA is literally an as-of join on CSV rows.
items.check: You can align a trade series to the most recent prior quote without an off-by-one look-ahead error.

items.know: Chained assignment and SettingWithCopyWarning. Silent index alignment in arithmetic. dtype coercion to object. Rolling windows that peek at the future. Timezone handling.
items.why: Silent index alignment will produce a wrong answer without an error, which is the worst failure mode. Tibra's rejection feedback asked explicitly for 'enhanced pandas library proficiency'.
items.check: You can state what happens when you add two Series with different indexes, without running it.

code.sub: Interviews ask you to translate mathematics into correct code under time pressure. This is that skill, isolated.

items.know: Normal equations, QR decomposition, and gradient descent. Compare their numerical behaviour on an ill-conditioned design. Add ridge and see the conditioning improve.
items.why: Two Sigma's signature OA family is exactly this: online no-intercept regression with a streaming slope update. Writing it correctly and stably is directly tested.
items.check: You can implement OLS three ways from scratch and explain which you would trust on ill-conditioned data.

items.know: Welford's online mean and variance. Online regression with rank-one updates. Exponentially weighted statistics. Two-heap streaming median.
items.why: Two Sigma asks for online regression; Quadrature asks for a streaming median estimator; Akuna asks for streaming max, mean and mode over a window. Live data arrives one tick at a time, so online forms are the native ones.
items.check: You can write a class that ingests one observation at a time and maintains mean, variance and a regression slope in O(1).

items.know: Piecewise linear interpolation and extrapolation. Newton's method and bisection for root-finding. Numerical integration. Optimisation via scipy.optimize, and when it fails.
items.why: Two Sigma's OA includes piecewise linear interpolation with large input sizes. WorldQuant asks for a square-root routine live. Implied volatility is a root-find, so this is also production code.
items.check: You can implement piecewise linear interpolation with correct extrapolation behaviour and O(log n) lookup.

items.t: Monte Carlo, and when not to use it
items.know: Sampling, convergence at root-n, antithetic variates and control variates for variance reduction. Seeding for reproducibility. Recognising when an exact dynamic-programming answer exists.
items.why: HRT explicitly criticised a Monte Carlo answer where exact dynamic programming was expected, on a dice-versus-coin probability question. Knowing when simulation is the lazy answer is the actual test.
items.check: Given a probability question, you can decide in under a minute whether exact computation is tractable.

code.sub: Turning an idea into evidence you would defend. This module decides full-time researcher take-homes.

items.know: Point-in-time data. Signal-to-position mapping with a lag you can justify. Transaction costs and slippage. Turnover. Capacity. Position sizing by inverse volatility.
items.why: Millennium's full-time QR take-home is a two-week end-to-end research pipeline. Schonfeld and Tibra both use signal-to-backtest cases. A backtest without costs is not a result.
items.check: You can state exactly where the one-bar lag between signal and position sits in your code, and why.

items.know: Why k-fold cross-validation is invalid on autocorrelated data. Walk-forward validation. Purging and embargoing around the test boundary. Keeping a genuine holdout untouched.
items.why: Standard scikit-learn cross-validation leaks future information into training on time series, which silently inflates every metric. Doing this correctly is rare and visible.
items.check: You can explain why a random train-test split on daily returns leaks, and describe the purge and embargo fix.

items.know: A six-part write-up: question, data, method, results, limitations, conclusion. In-sample and out-of-sample side by side. Net-of-cost metrics. Stating the number of variants you tried.
items.why: The documented take-home rejections in this research were all about judgement, not code: analysing variables in isolation, using correlation instead of predictive power, and presenting in-sample results without caveats. G-Research reviews your take-home as a code review with you.
items.check: Your write-up states how many hypotheses you tested before the one you are presenting.

items.know: Seeded randomness, pinned dependencies, a deterministic pipeline from raw data to figure, version control with meaningful commits.
items.why: A result you cannot reproduce is not a result. Also the difference between a take-home that reads as professional and one that reads as a notebook dump.
items.check: Someone else can clone your take-home and regenerate every number with one command.

code.sub: Deliberately narrow. This exists to get you past automated screens, not to make you a competitive programmer.

items.know: Hash maps and counting. Two pointers and sliding windows. Sorting with custom keys. Binary search including on the answer. Stacks, queues and heaps. Breadth-first and depth-first search. Straightforward dynamic programming. Intervals.
items.why: These cover essentially every reported researcher-track online assessment in the database. Qube, Akuna, Rokos and Maven all sit at LeetCode-medium within these patterns.
items.check: You can solve an unseen LeetCode medium in 25 minutes, in Python, with correct edge cases.

items.know: Time and space complexity stated before you code. Recognising when an O(n^2) approach will time out at the stated constraints.
items.why: Citadel gives no partial credit for solutions that time out; HRT requires all hidden tests to pass. Reading the constraints tells you the intended complexity before you start.
items.check: Given n up to 200,000, you immediately know O(n^2) is excluded and O(n log n) is the target.

code.sub: Narrow but genuinely load-bearing at one specific cluster of firms.

items.know: Joins of every kind, group by with having, common table expressions, and window functions: row_number, rank, lag, lead, and rolling aggregates over partitions.
items.why: Point72 is the clearest case: its quant analyst assessment is three Python questions and one SQL, and the intern version is two SQL out of five. Marshall Wace ends with a SQL schema interview; Man AHL and Tower both test it.
items.check: You can write a query returning each asset's return ranked within its sector by date, using window functions only.

exclude.why: Sigma-algebras, Radon-Nikodym derivatives and formal martingale theory appear in no reported interview in this research outside PhD research presentations, and are not used in daily statistical-arbitrage work. If you have it from a maths degree it costs nothing to keep; acquiring it deliberately for interviews is months misspent.

exclude.t: Full stochastic calculus, for non-options roles
exclude.why: SDEs, Girsanov, Feynman-Kac and numerical PDE methods are the toolkit of a derivatives pricing quant. For statistical-arbitrage and systematic research they are close to irrelevant. Module S7 above gives the ceiling you need for options market makers; going deeper is only justified if you are specifically targeting a vol desk.

Transformers, CNNs and the current architecture zoo appear in this research only at ML-specialist tracks such as G-Research's ML Engineer and XTX's research roles. For a general QR role, a strong grasp of regularised linear models and gradient boosting dominates a shallow familiarity with neural networks, because the signal-to-noise ratio in returns rarely supports high-capacity models.

Segment trees, Fenwick trees, suffix automata, heavy-light decomposition. Absent from every first-hand researcher-track round in the 198-question database. The one exception, union-find, appeared twice, so learn that one and stop.

Prep sites claim you need a 2400+ rating. Tower's own intern assessment states 1600-1800 and every first-person report agrees. Rating above that buys nothing for a research role and costs hundreds of hours.

Spark, Hadoop, Kafka and Kubernetes are not tested in any reported researcher-track loop here. They appear only in platform engineering roles such as G-Research's Kubernetes questions. Learn them on the job if your team uses them.

exclude.t: CFA curriculum and general corporate finance
exclude.why: Accounting, valuation, WACC and capital structure have no presence in the reported quant research or trading loops. This is discretionary finance content and it is not what these firms test.

exclude.t: C++ depth, for the research track specifically
exclude.why: Radix and some HFT research roles require C++, so check your target list. But for the systematic-fund cluster including Two Sigma, DE Shaw, Millennium, Point72, Man AHL and G-Research, Python fluency dominates and C++ depth is not tested. Do not spend a month on move semantics for a Python research role.

For trader roles probability practice is essential, but rote-memorising puzzle books generalises badly because interviewers deliberately change assumptions mid-problem. Jane Street's rounds are built to defeat memorisation. Learn the underlying method: first-step analysis, martingales, indicators, symmetry.

seq.d: Module S1 and S2 only. Work problems daily under time pressure; the target is speed and reliability, not coverage. In parallel, 30 minutes a day on module C6 patterns so the assessment gate never becomes the bottleneck.
seq.gate: You can solve an unseen medium probability problem in five minutes and an unseen LeetCode medium in twenty-five.

seq.d: Modules S3 and S4 alongside C1, C2 and C4. Every statistical result you learn, implement from scratch the same week. Deriving OLS and then coding it three ways in the same sitting is the point.
seq.gate: You can derive OLS on paper, implement it stably in numpy, and explain what robust standard errors fix.

seq.d: Modules S5 and S6 with C3. This is where general statistics becomes finance. Work with real price data throughout, not synthetic examples.
seq.gate: You can take a raw price file to a validated, cost-aware signal evaluation without a look-ahead error.

seq.d: Module C5 applied. Produce a single polished piece of research with a six-part write-up, honest out-of-sample results, and a stated count of variants tried. This doubles as your take-home rehearsal and your portfolio.
seq.gate: A stranger can clone your repository, run one command, and reproduce every figure.

seq.t: Options, only if targeting a vol desk
seq.d: Module S7. Add only if Optiver, IMC, SIG, Akuna, Da Vinci or Jane Street trading is on your list. Skip entirely for pure statistical-arbitrage research.
seq.gate: You can derive Black-Scholes from a binomial limit and state put-call parity from memory.

res.n: The best route to module S1. Harvard's Stat 110 lectures are free on YouTube and follow the book exactly.

res.t: Xinfeng Zhou, A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews
res.n: Known universally as the Green Book. The standard interview problem set for probability and brainteasers. Work it, do not read it.
Fast and rigorous coverage of module S3. Suited to someone with mathematical maturity who wants inference without a two-semester detour.
Free online and genuinely rigorous. The reference for module S4, especially robust and HAC standard errors, which most machine-learning texts skip entirely.

res.t: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning
res.n: Chapters 1 to 9 cover regularisation, model selection and validation. XTX has reportedly pointed candidates at exactly this range.

res.t: Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series
res.n: Module S5 in one book: stationarity, ARMA, GARCH, cointegration, with financial examples rather than macroeconomic ones.
G-Research's official preparation guidance recommends the first four chapters. Source of the fundamental law of active management and the alpha/risk-model separation.

res.t: Stefanica, Radoicic & Wang, 150 Most Frequently Asked Questions on Quant Interviews
res.n: G-Research states its own sample exam sits at this level, which makes it a calibration tool as much as a problem set.

res.t: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning
res.n: Contested as a whole, but the chapters on purged and embargoed cross-validation, and on backtest overfitting, are the clearest treatment of module C5 validation anywhere. Read those chapters; be sceptical of the rest.
Written by the author of pandas. The efficient path through module C3, including the alignment semantics that cause silent errors.
For module C2's numerical care: conditioning, QR, SVD and why you never invert a matrix. Short, and unusually well written for the subject.
